Voat has some major issues. For example, it's recently been plagued by vote manipulators, hit with Micro$hekel fees, etc., and there are more underlying issues which I think are important. I created Freeboard in an attempt to fix them.

What I think is wrong with Voat (and solutions)

  1. The voting system. It's too easy to manipulate. If someone wanted to get a post onto the top of the front page, it's only a matter of 1 hour of clicking buttons and solving captchas -- and this can't really be solved easily, since the solutions involve either sophisticated tracking of users (which would be a potential invasion of privacy), or increasing the restrictions on new accounts (which would drive away users). In addition, downvotes help to remove or reduce the visibility of any content which users don't like. Sometimes this means that spam gets pushed to the bottom (good), but in a significant portion of cases, this affects opinions which are generally disliked. Please note that I generally don't support SJWs and such, but I do believe that hiding people based on their opinions is counterproductive.

  2. CCP restrictions. They are definitely useful for stopping people who post the same crap over and over again, but they are also very effective in silencing people who are the target of a brigade, or people who have unpopular opinions. Once CCP becomes negative, it's hard to bring it back to positive due to posting restrictions.

  3. User accounts. Opinions should gain or lose acceptance based on their content, not on who said them. For example, if @puttitout says something, people are going to be much more accepting of his statements than if someone hated (e.g. @sanegoatiswear) said the same thing. The solution to this problem is to make everyone anonymous, or at least identified by a random ID (to prevent samefagging).

  4. Reliance on proprietary software and JavaScript. @puttitout is attempting to switch Voat to free software, but that will take a very long time. Freeboard is free software and uses free software exclusively. In addition to the whole problem with Microsoft, there is a Google captcha applied to all low-CCP users and Tor users, and this requires proprietary JavaScript to run, which is prohibitive when one does not want to run proprietary software on their computers. On top of that, JavaScript in general is essentially required to use Voat. Freeboard fixes this problem by using very little JavaScript (and the little JavaScript that is used is only for convenience), and also providing RSS feeds in place of the AJAX notifications. This is helpful to command line people (like me) and Tor users.

Freeboard also has public deletion logs, like on Voat. This (as you all know) makes it difficult for moderators to silently delete content.

Here it is: http://freeboard.zapto.org

If you think the above points have merit, feel free to make some threads and discussions on Freeboard.

I agree with the problems you identify in points 1 and 2. There are behaviors and structures on voat which do prevent it from actually being the free speech platform it could be. But it is still better than most alternatives. I will be curious how well your site works.

On point 3, I disagree somewhat. While I understand the point you are making I think it is outweighed by the ability to establish credibility as an account with a consistently good or bad track record. Let's face it, some people's credibility is higher than others for good reason. Some people have expertise that few others have. Et cetera. If every post were completely anonymous, it would destroy our ability to quickly integrate information and apply appropriate filters based on knowledge of the speaker.

On point 4, I am agnostic. As long as a site works for me, I am happy.

I agree with a lot of what you say, but I like having up and downvotes. Yes, they reduce the visibility of some content, but the ordering is useful/interesting/time-saving and a large part of why reddit-like sites are so appealing (I really appreciate being able to order from the bottom around here, and additional functionality along those lines could be added). If your website does not restrict user rights (the ability to post, upvote, downvote, comment) based on popularity (CCP) I don't see a reason to throw away up and downvotes altogether for posts and comments. If anything you might want to expand on the system, and include a third class of vote for obvious spam. If spam becomes a problem, you might want to restrict the number of posts or comments for every single user, or make it progressively more difficult (more captcha) for people to post for the 10th time versus the first time in a day... I think spam is a weak excuse for censorship around here and would love to be able to verify methods of minimising it without censoring ideas and creating a popular circlejerk.
